findings.text: The first sentence says plainly what Athena is and what makes it different, so a newcomer can name the product within seconds.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page says why it exists: it shows Athena's work instead of only describing it. The [c1]-style links to file and line sources make that promise something a reader can check.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: Athena's main job, per the lede, is turning a request into a code change. This page shows a different kind of output, a study, and never shows a request turned into a change or the cost record the lede promises. A newcomer sees a side capability, not the core one.
findings.source: Header: "Athena turns a short request into a change to a code repository" vs. the rest of the page (a study of firstmate)

findings.text: Almost all of the page is detailed firstmate internals: exit codes, lock behaviour, pending-close replays. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena will likely skim or give up well before the Next steps section, though the early "Next step" link in the header softens this.
findings.source: Headings "States of a piece of work", "Counters", "Transitions", "Claims and sources" (44 claims)

findings.text: The "Start here" section is well built. It says what firstmate is in one sentence, defines the terms it relies on before using them, and follows one task from start to finish.
Some definitions are circular or thin: "wake" is never defined, and the ship entry says little on its own. "endpoint", "heartbeat" and "brief" are used in transitions and claims but never defined.
findings.source: Glossary: "stale wake — A wake after which the agent inspects a worker..."; "ship — A kind of task, named next to scouts."

findings.text: The next steps are concrete. But they skip how to get the checkout and what is needed first (a Rust toolchain, model API access), so a newcomer may stall before the first command works.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page is open about what it does not know and about the fact that nothing was run. That builds trust in the claims it does make.
findings.source: "in scope — ... The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."; Limits of this study f1: "no failure or retry edge was observed"

findings.text: This exposes Athena's internal process history (an earlier pass missed things). A newcomer gains little from it, and it may raise doubts without saying what was done to fix it.
findings.source: Limits of this study f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths..."

findings.text: The page does not say which repository `studies/` is in (Athena's or firstmate's), so a newcomer cannot follow this pointer without guessing.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"
